title: Impact of workplace health interventions on the cardiovascular risk profile: A controlled longitudinal study.
summary:
Background: The risk of cardiovascular diseases such as heart attack or stroke can be reduced by adopting a healthy lifestyle with sufficient exercise and a balanced diet. Workplace health promotion programs are designed to help employees live healthier lives. However, it is still unclear how effective different programs actually are.

Research question: This study examines whether and to what extent various workplace health programs can reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. The Framingham Risk Score, which calculates an individual's risk of heart attack or stroke over the next 10 years, is used for this purpose.

Methodology: 240 employees aged between 40 and 65 are participating in the study. They are divided into four groups: three groups are taking part in health programs of varying intensity (a 4-day seminar, 11-day compact training course, or 21-day classic training course). A control group is not receiving any structured program. At the beginning of the study, after completion of the programs, and after 6 weeks and 6 months, various health values are measured: blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, body weight, and fitness. In addition, participants complete questionnaires on their health behavior, quality of life, and ability to work. Fitness is measured using a novel, painless method in which a small sensor on the sternum records heart movements (seismocardiography). After the programs, half of the participants are randomly selected to receive additional individual health coaching. This allows researchers to investigate whether this coaching helps to maintain the positive effects in the long term.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Written informed consent.

Willingness to participate in physical activity and non-invasive measurements.

Availability for follow-up examinations over a period of 6 months.
Exclusion criteria:
Manifest cardiovascular diseases (e.g., history of heart attack, bypass, stent, heart valve replacement, pacemaker).

Poorly controlled chronic respiratory diseases (asthma/COPD).

Severe orthopedic limitations.

Pregnancy.

Use of performance-influencing medication (e.g., beta blockers).

Severe mental illness.

Planned extended absences (e.g., sabbatical, secondment).

Above-average fitness level (>2x endurance training or >3x sports/week).
